deep_dive.title: MAS-BIT: A Multi-Agent System for End-to-End BraIn-to-Text Decoding
deep_dive.abstract: Speech brain-computer interfaces aim to restore communication by translating neural activity into text, yet end-to-end decoders have historically trailed cascaded systems in accuracy. We introduce a Multi-Agent System for BraIn-to-Text (MAS-BIT), the first multi-agent framework for end-to-end brain-to-text decoding from intracortical recordings. MAS-BIT coordinates three specialized agents: a neural agent that interprets continuous neural representations, a phonetic agent that decodes soft phoneme posteriors, and an arbitration agent that integrates their complementary evidence with direct access to neural representations to generate the final transcription. The expert agents communicate with the arbiter through token-embedding-based latent communication, constructing continuous messages as probability-weighted combinations of token embeddings. These messages retain alternative token hypotheses and provide a differentiable interface through which sentence-level supervision jointly trains the neural encoders and specialized agents across participants. MAS-BIT achieves state-of-the-art end-to-end decoding performance on the Brain-to-Text '24 and '25 benchmarks, with word error rates of 6.929% on '24 and 3.606% on the '25 public test set (3.892% on the private test set). These results surpass the published BIT cascade on the '25 public set and narrow the gap on '24, without ensembling independently trained models or using external language-model rescoring.

deep_dive.title: State of Mind: Learning and Evaluating World Models of Naturalistic Brain Dynamics
deep_dive.abstract: Understanding naturalistic brain activity requires going beyond the stimulus alone, as external inputs continuously interact with an individual's evolving brain state. A world model captures such dynamics in a latent state by inferring it from neural observations, predicting stimulus-driven evolution, and updating with new observations. However, existing brain world models fail to maintain a persistent latent state over time, and standard metrics of neural prediction accuracy cannot tell whether a model tracks an individual's brain state or relies solely on the stimulus. To directly test state inference, prediction, and updating, we introduce BrainStateBench, which evaluates a model's latent state through a frozen linear probe on whole-cortex, movie-driven fMRI. Its State task tests whether a model captures trial-to-trial variability in an individual's responses to repeated stimuli, while Forecast and Updating evaluate future activity predictions without and with new observations, respectively. To track individual brain state across time, we propose Spectator, a linear latent world model trained with a joint-embedding predictive objective. Spectator encodes short- and long-horizon observation histories into a two-timescale latent state and predicts state transitions linearly from the current state and stimulus. Stimulus-only encoders reach 0.320 in fMRI prediction correlation without observing the brain (0% on State), while prior deep brain world models reach 0.239 yet score at most 0.4% on State. In contrast, Spectator achieves 0.349 correlation alongside 5.5% on State, 16.0% on Forecast, and 20.3% on Updating, outperforming all baselines while forecasting over 20x faster than deep forecasting models.

deep_dive.title: SENSA: Visual-to-Brain Generation with Individualized Subject-State Transfer and Adaptation
deep_dive.abstract: Visual-to-brain encoding predicts neural responses to visual stimuli, supporting visual cognition research and neural decoding. However, challenges in disentangling shared from image-specific activity, together with inter-subject distribution shifts and representational heterogeneity, limit accurate encoding and cross-subject generalization with limited calibration data.   We introduce SENSA, a structured continuous neural response generation framework that separates shared activity from image-dependent responses and calibrates a compact subject state. An independent response prior captures shared activity, while complementary visual descriptors drive separable sensor-time bases and a shared Response Refiner. Subject-Adaptive Factor Transport adjusts the spatiotemporal expression of shared bases, while Source-Grounded Residual Memory predicts image-dependent corrections in source-response coordinates. Together, they personalize a frozen generator using limited paired support.   Experiments demonstrate that the generation backbone outperforms recent generators across three datasets, with image-identity perturbations confirming stimulus specificity. Using only 400 paired images, electroencephalography (EEG) and the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) calibration achieve residual Pearson correlations of 0.1091 and 0.2995, respectively, demonstrating effective brain-response generation and cross-subject adaptation.

deep_dive.title: STAGE: Structured Test-Time Adaptation with Global Entropic Soft-coupling for Cross-Subject Brain-to-Image Retrieval
deep_dive.abstract: Cross-subject brain-to-image retrieval aims to identify viewed images from unseen subjects' brain signals. However, inter-subject variability hinders alignment of brain-image representations, while independent query ranking tends to concentrate predictions on a few candidates, making accurate retrieval difficult without target labels. We propose STAGE (Structured Test-Time Adaptation with Global Entropic Soft-coupling), a structured test-time adaptation framework for recovering cross-subject alignment from uncertain brain-image correspondences. Moment calibration reduces statistical discrepancies between features, while coupling-weighted initialization establishes initial alignment. Coupling-guided adaptation further refines residual feature mismatches, and soft-coupling ranking coordinates candidate competition across queries to prevent overly concentrated matching assignments. Using only unlabeled target batches, STAGE maintains consistent matching from feature calibration to image retrieval while keeping both encoders frozen. Experiments on three public datasets validate STAGE's retrieval performance. On THINGS-EEG2, STAGE achieves 68.25% Top-1 and 90.47% Top-5, improving Top-1 by 18.52 percentage points over SCORE recovery and CSLS on identical frozen NICE features. Calibrated on 200 queries and a 200-image gallery covering their identities, STAGE retains 42.05% Top-1 when ranking 1,854 images with the transform frozen.

deep_dive.title: EVD-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for EEG-to-Image Decoding
deep_dive.abstract: EEG-to-image decoding recovers visual information from non-invasive brain recordings, providing a window into human perception. However, comparisons across systems are confounded by a variable that is rarely reported as such: which participants' data the system was allowed to use. The same Top-1 score on a 200-way gallery may come from a per-participant system, a pooled model over all participants, or a model that never saw the test participant---cases that differ by more than most architectural changes between the methods being compared. We present \bench, a benchmark on THINGS-EEG2 that standardizes the gallery and EEG input, matches training budgets across systems within each regime, and compares three participant-access regimes: within-subject, joint-subject, and strict leave-one-subject-out, with unlabeled target calibration reported separately. All three settings evaluate concept-level zero-shot retrieval: the 200 test concepts are disjoint from the 1,654 concepts used for EEG--image fitting and validation. We compare retrieval across access regimes and use zero-EEG and matched-wrong EEG controls to assess dependence on correct EEG--stimulus pairing. We vary trial averaging, gallery size and difficulty, and training data coverage, and compare target adaptation and visual feature targets. We also assess sensitivity to EEG window length and channel count, robustness to input perturbations, and confidence calibration. These results establish participant-access regime as a necessary reporting dimension alongside gallery, repetition, and visual target.

quick_skim.title: A generative framework for unified representations bridging electrophysiological and haemodynamic brain activity
quick_skim.abstract: Electrophysiological and haemodynamic recordings resolve brain activity at complementary temporal and spatial scales, yet paired acquisition remains difficult to scale. We propose a generative framework that aligns paired multimodal recordings in a unified representation space and generates modality-specific haemodynamic responses from EEG. In paired cohorts, the framework generated fMRI BOLD and fNIRS haemoglobin responses that reproduced regional dynamics, cortical maps, functional connectivity and task structure. Generated BOLD followed Real BOLD time courses and cortical patterns, while Generated haemoglobin responses tracked task-evoked HbO and HbR dynamics. The framework enabled decoding across visual, motor-imagery and mental-arithmetic tasks, independent-record decoding, external BOLD localization and low-sample augmentation. Paired feature-space calibration supported bidirectional retrieval. The proposed framework extends cortical analysis and brain decoding to EEG recordings when Real haemodynamic data are sparse.

quick_skim.title: History-bearing thalamocortical signals reconstruct and redirect later decisions in a circuit model
quick_skim.abstract: Experience can guide an ambiguous choice or bias a choice despite strong current evidence. We asked how a thalamocortical circuit carries historical content forward and regulates its influence across successive decisions. In published data from adult male mice, suppressing posterior parietal cortex (PPC) or pulvinar (PUL) improved current judgments most when sensory history conflicted with the stimulus, reflecting reduced historical weighting. In trained thalamocortical circuit models, replaying recorded PUL input to PPC reconstructed a historical trace after equalizing complete recipient states across histories. Replaying the opposite history redirected the later choice, even after the circuit correctly judged an intervening strong stimulus. This historical message occupied a low-dimensional direction in thalamic output that remained broadly reachable under firing-rate bounds; redistributing the arriving current at matched energy showed that fine spatial organization, beyond total input strength, selectively shapes later history use without disrupting current choices. Strong sensory evidence suppressed historical output while preserving internal state differences, whereas ambiguity recruited neuronal rectification thresholds and readout alignment to express history. Small shifts in the cortical operating point modulated later historical influence, and partial attenuation of recurrent drive reduced it across all circuits while preserving current commitments; correspondingly, recurrent dynamics were essential for predicting post-stimulus trajectories in held-out histories. Together, these findings distinguish three operations in history-guided choice: returning thalamocortical input determines which past is reconstructed, recurrent dynamics carry its influence forward across intervening demands, and current sensory evidence gates how strongly it enters the decision.

quick_skim.title: Spiking Neural Networks Incrementally Track Firing-Rate Networks
quick_skim.abstract: Understanding how spiking neural networks (SNNs) efficiently process data streams is key to (i) studying how biological brains conserve energy for lifelong predictions and (ii) enabling efficient continuous AI inference. In this work, we propose a theory on how an SNN incrementally tracks its corresponding firing-rate network, a continuous-valued neural network (ANN). We prove that the output of a discrete SNN continuously tracks the instantaneous ANN output implicitly determined by the SNN input. Based on this principle, we develop LIF-Stream, a conversion framework for efficient SNN inference over unbounded data streams. It enables the converted SNN to reuse its prior activation state and compute only the activation updates between frames, thereby reducing the average number of time steps needed per frame. Specifically, LIF-Stream controls the SNN to continuously track the reference ANN output, which gives a high-accuracy prediction for every frame. Evaluation on three large-scale streaming inference benchmarks with distinct modalities shows that LIF-Stream achieves the best efficiency-accuracy trade-off compared to high-accuracy SNN techniques.

quick_skim.title: Beyond Full-Context Accuracy: Context-Marginalized Evaluation of Test-Time Structure-Aware Inference in EEG-to-Image Retrieval
quick_skim.abstract: Test-time structure-aware inference can improve cross-subject EEG-to-image retrieval by exploiting relations among unlabeled test queries, but it also makes predictions depend on query-set composition. Existing evaluations typically report accuracy under a single full-query context, leaving unclear whether gains and comparative conclusions hold as context changes. We introduce Context-Marginalized Retrieval Evaluation (CMRE), which repeatedly evaluates each target query in sampled contexts using the corresponding rows of a fixed query-gallery similarity matrix. CMRE distinguishes structural exploitability, quantified by gains over independent retrieval, from context robustness, measured by same-query Top-1 context consistency. Under leave-one-subject-out evaluation on THINGS-EEG2 across six frozen representations and six structure-aware inference rules, structure-aware inference improves full-context Top-1 accuracy by up to 20.40 percentage points over independent retrieval. However, the rule selected under full-context evaluation is no longer optimal in 17 of 24 representation-context-size conditions (70.8%). Selecting the full-context winner incurs an average loss of 2.70 percentage points and a maximum loss of 8.29 percentage points under reduced contexts. Representation rankings are likewise inference- and context-dependent: the ordering under independent retrieval is not consistently preserved under structure-aware inference. Moreover, larger retrieval gains do not necessarily imply greater context robustness, showing that retrieval effectiveness and prediction stability provide complementary views of structure-aware inference. Full-context accuracy captures one operating point of context-dependent inference. CMRE complements it by characterizing how structural gains, context consistency, and comparisons of rules and representations change with query context.
quick_skim.llm_tldr_en: Introduces context-marginalized evaluation for cross-subject EEG-to-image retrieval, disentangling structural gains and robustness.

quick_skim.title: PhyMind: Physics-Informed Masked Autoencoding for EEG Foundation Models
quick_skim.abstract: EEG foundation models are pre-trained almost exclusively with masked reconstruction through a free-form decoder, sometimes with hand-crafted spectral targets added, as in MANAS-2. We study what happens when that decoder is replaced by a generative forward model of EEG. PhyMind keeps a standard masked transformer encoder, but its decoder must explain the masked signal through 68 cortical regions, each driven by damped stochastic oscillators and an aperiodic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, projected to the recording's own montage by a fixed boundary-element lead field evaluated per derivation. Training combines masked reconstruction with a Whittle spectral likelihood, an oscillator-dynamics residual, a minimum-norm source prior and a penalised neural residual. In a controlled comparison (same encoder, data, steps and seed), the physics decoder produces encoder tokens whose spectral content is far more linearly decodable than with a masked-autoencoder decoder or with the MANAS-2 objective: mean R^2 on a token-level spectral probe with amplitude-normalised targets is 0.67/0.77/0.77 on three datasets, against 0.24/0.50/0.50 (MAE) and 0.48/0.67/0.66 (MANAS-2 objective), approaching the released 92.8M-parameter MANAS-2 (0.71/0.81/0.80). Downstream gains in the controlled setting are small (four-task mean balanced accuracy 56.6 vs. 53.8 for MAE frozen, 63.8 vs. 62.7 fine-tuned). Region-level features from the physics decoder raise frozen four-class motor-imagery accuracy by 7-14 points, so a 7.2M-parameter model pre-trained on 3k hours of open EEG is comparable to the released MANAS-2 with frozen features (63.0 vs. 61.6). After full fine-tuning, MANAS-2 remains better (66.8 vs. 65.4 for our best model). The inferred sources do not reproduce the lateralisation that a classical inverse solution finds in motor imagery, so we do not claim anatomical interpretability. Code and weights are released.

quick_skim.title: Second-Order Dynamics in Noisy RNNs Produce Exploration and Temporal Compression in Replay
quick_skim.abstract: Biological neural networks (like the hippocampus) can internally generate "replay" resembling stimulus-driven activity. Recent computational models of replay use noisy recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained to path-integrate. Replay in these networks is described as Langevin sampling, but this theory alone fails to capture the environmental exploration and temporal compression observed in real biological replay. To close this gap, we re-examine spontaneous noisy RNN activity ("replay") as Langevin sampling, one timestep at a time, from a time-series distribution resembling lived experiences (unlike previous works which defined sampling as Monte Carlo inference over a static distribution). We provide a normative second-order Langevin sampling framework wherein spike-frequency adaptation drives spatial exploration at the cost of speed, and momentum via dendritic input differentiation drives temporal compression. We numerically verify our framework via simulations of noisy RNNs trained on 2D triangular and T-maze navigation activity, and others trained on place cell activity of synthetic rats. Crucially, we observe that simultaneous adaptation and momentum increases both replay exploration and speed, and provide one of the first accounts for biologically plausible temporal compression in rate-based RNN replay. Our findings encourage experiments into whether dendritic input differentiation, or other mechanisms, may support temporal compression in memory circuits like the hippocampus.
quick_skim.llm_evidence_en: noisy RNNs produce exploration and temporal compression in replay

quick_skim.title: SleepXA: Composing Pretrained Neural and Cardiac Foundation Models for Sleep Representation Learning
quick_skim.abstract: Physiological signals recorded during sleep provide synchronized views of neural, cardiac, respiratory, and other bodily systems, while preserving modality-specific information. Existing EEG and ECG foundation models already capture rich but distinct physiological structure, motivating an alternative to training a multimodal sleep model from scratch: composing existing pretrained models. We introduce SleepXA, a framework that uses synchronized polysomnography (PSG) to compose independently pretrained neural and cardiac foundation models. SleepXA combines pretrained EEG and ECG encoders with lightweight encoders for additional PSG modalities, and learns shared and modality-specific representations through sleep-guided alignment. We pretrain SleepXA on 9,230 overnight PSG recordings from three large cohorts and evaluate it on 27 downstream tasks spanning sleep representation, clinical and disease prediction, and daytime physiological transfer. SleepXA ranks among the top two methods on 22 of 27 tasks. Controlled experiments further show consistent benefits across sensor configurations and EEG-ECG backbone choices, while pretrained initialization outperforms architecture-matched training from scratch and SleepXA surpasses alternative multimodal composition strategies. These results suggest that synchronized multimodal physiology can serve as a natural interface for composing existing physiological foundation models, yielding reusable representations that extend beyond sleep to clinical and daytime physiological settings.
quick_skim.llm_evidence_en: composing pretrained neural and cardiac foundation models for sleep representation learning from EEG
